contentBlocks.text: Bounce a ball straight down and it comes straight back up, over and over. Swing on a swing and you go back and forth in the same path every time. Motion often follows a pattern — and once you know the pattern, you can predict what happens next.

Scientists look for patterns in motion to make predictions. Try this: bounce a ball straight down five times and watch closely. Does it bounce the same height each time, or a little lower? Now roll a toy car across the floor and let it stop on its own. Try it three times from the same starting push — does it stop in about the same place each time? A repeating pattern (like the swing's back-and-forth path) lets you predict future motion. An object slowing down due to friction is also a pattern — you can predict it will eventually stop.

By watching a pattern carefully, you can predict what an object will do next — that's exactly what scientists do with real motion data. Tomorrow we'll investigate a force that works without even touching anything: magnetism.

objectives: Make observations of an object's motion to identify a repeating pattern
Use an observed pattern to predict future motion
materialsNeeded: A small toy car or ball that can roll
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Ask: have you ever noticed something move the same way over and over?
2. Do the ball-bounce investigation together — bounce 5 times, discuss whether the height pattern is exactly the same or gradually shrinks (it shrinks — energy is lost each bounce, a good informal preview, no need to name 'energy' formally here).
3. Do the rolling-car investigation 3 times from the same push, comparing stopping distance.
4. Discuss the swing example as a clean back-and-forth pattern.
5. Complete the worksheet: given a description of a pattern, predict what happens next.
6. Close by asking the child to name one more repeating-motion pattern from daily life (a ceiling fan, a clock's second hand, footsteps).
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus only on the swing example (simplest, most familiar pattern) before comparing it to the ball bounce
Ready for more: discuss why the ball bounces a little lower each time instead of exactly the same height every time
Hands-on learners should do all three investigations themselves, not just watch
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. A swing goes back and forth — next it will swing forward again. 2. A ball bounced repeatedly gets a little lower each time — next bounce will be slightly lower than the last. 3. A car rolling and slowing down will eventually stop. 4. A clock's second hand moves in a repeating circle — it will keep going around.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS 3-PS2-2: making observations and/or measurements of an object's motion to provide evidence that a pattern can be used to predict future motion.

generationData.instructions: Read each pattern. Write what will most likely happen next.

rows.problem: A swing goes back and forth. It just swung backward. What happens next?
A ball is bounced and gets a little lower each bounce. What happens on the next bounce?
A toy car rolls and slows down a little more each second. What eventually happens?
A clock's second hand moves in a repeating circle. What will it keep doing?
